images.caption: Balaklava, section of the city of Sevastopol, on the Crimean peninsula. Fishing and limestone quarrying are carried on. In ancient times it was an important Greek commercial city. In the Middle Ages it belonged to the Genoese until it was taken (1475) by the Turks, who gave it its present name. Balaklava was the capital of the former Balaklava district in the Crimean region until 1957, when it was incorporated into Sevastopol. There are ruins of a Genoese fortress (14th-15th cent.) in Balaklava.
images.alt: Balaklava, section of the city of Sevastopol, on the Crimean peninsula. Fishing and limestone quarrying are carried on. In ancient times it was an important Greek commercial city. In the Middle Ages it belonged to the Genoese until it was taken (1475) by the Turks, who gave it its present name. images.caption: This satellite image highlights the jagged coastline of the southern Crimean Peninsula and the various docking areas of Sevastopol. The urban area is light grey, and it is bounded to the north and west by the Black Sea, to the south by vegetated (light green) and fallow (tan) agricultural fields, and to the east by the city of Inkerman and vegetated uplands (deep green). The city of Balaklava, to the south, houses another relic of the Cold War—an underground Soviet submarine base that is now open to the public as a monument. The Chernaya River issues into the Black Sea near Inkerman, flowing into the Sevastopol Inlet to the west.

images.caption:
Source of data: Federal State Statistics Service of Russia (Rosstat), Unified Interdepartmental Information and Statistical System of Russia.
In the lower chart, about difference in life expectancy between urban and rural types of settlements for the entire population, for males and for females, in some places there is an apparent paradox that the difference for the entire population is smaller than specifically for males and females. This is due to the different proportions of males and females - the proportion of females in urban is lower. A larger proportion of females in rural pulls the lower (rural) limit of total statistics up. And a larger proportion of males in urban pulls the upper (urban) limit of total statistics down. Thus, the gap for the total statistics is smaller than the gap for males and females separately.
images.alt:
Source of data: Federal State Statistics Service of Russia (Rosstat), Unified Interdepartmental Information and Statistical System of Russia.

This is due to the different proportions of males and females - the proportion of females in urban is lower. A larger proportion of females in rural pulls the lower (rural) limit of total statistics up. And a larger proportion of males in urban pulls the upper (urban) limit of total statistics down. Thus, the gap for the total statistics is smaller than the gap for males and females separately.

images.filename: Life expectancy in Russian subject -Crimea and its parts.png
images.caption:
Life expectancy for Crimea is calculated as the average value of life expectancy in the Republic of Crimea and the federal city of Sevastopol, taking into account the population in these subjects of Russia in the middle of the corresponding years, according to data of Rosstat. 
Rosstat provides in the public domain data on number of the population in the subjects on average, for urban and rural areas, but does not provide data on number of males and females. Therefore, the life expectancy of males and females in Crimea on average was calculated based on the assumption that their proportions in the Republic of Crimea and Sevastopol are the same. This is not strictly true, but the difference is insignificant and not noticeable on the chart visually.

Source of data for life expectancy: Federal State Statistics Service of Russia (Rosstat), Unified Interdepartmental Information and Statistical System of Russia

Source of data for number of population: Federal State Statistics Service of Russia (Rosstat)
